questions.q: Explain why \(\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\) does not exist.
questions.target: Limits that fail to exist and the squeeze theorem
questions.answer: As \(x \rightarrow 0\), \(\frac{1}{x} \rightarrow \pm\infty\), so \(\sin(1/x)\) oscillates between \(-1\) and \(1\) infinitely often near \(x = 0\) rather than approaching a single value.
questions.explanation: As \(x \rightarrow 0\), \(\frac{1}{x} \rightarrow \pm\infty\), so \(\sin(1/x)\) oscillates between \(-1\) and \(1\) infinitely often near \(x = 0\) rather than approaching a single value.

questions.q: Use the squeeze theorem to evaluate \(\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} x^2\cos\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\).
questions.target: Limits that fail to exist and the squeeze theorem
questions.answer: Since \(-x^2 \leq x^2\cos(1/x) \leq x^2\) and \(\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}(\pm x^2) = 0\), the squeeze theorem gives a limit of \(0\).
questions.explanation: Since \(-x^2 \leq x^2\cos(1/x) \leq x^2\) and \(\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}(\pm x^2) = 0\), the squeeze theorem gives a limit of \(0\).

questions.q: For \(f(x)=2x+1\) if \(x<3\), and \(f(x)=x^2-2\) if \(x\geq3\), evaluate \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3^-}f(x)\) and \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3^+}f(x)\), and state whether \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3}f(x)\) exists.
questions.target: Limits with absolute value and piecewise functions
questions.answer: \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3^-}f(x)=2(3)+1=7\). \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3^+}f(x)=3^2-2=7\). Since both one-sided limits equal \(7\), \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3}f(x)=7\) exists.
questions.explanation: \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3^-}f(x)=2(3)+1=7\). \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3^+}f(x)=3^2-2=7\). Since both one-sided limits equal \(7\), \(\lim_{x\rightarrow3}f(x)=7\) exists.

questions.q: Level 3 · Advanced Evaluate the improper integral or establish its divergence: \(\int_0^\infty x e^{-x/2}\,dx\)
questions.answer: Express as a limit of a definite integral: \(\int_0^\infty x e^{-x/2}\,dx = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \int_0^t x e^{-x/2}\,dx\) Integrate by parts on \([0, t]\): Let \(u = x \Rightarrow du = dx\), and \(dv = e^{-x/2}dx \Rightarrow v = -2e^{-x/2}\). \(\int_0^t x e^{-x/2}\,dx = \left[ -2x e^{-x/2} \right]_0^t - \int_0^t (-2e^{-x/2})\,dx = -2t e^{-t/2} + 0 + 2 \left[ -2e^{-x/2} \right]_0^t\) \(= -2t e^{-t/2} - 4(e^{-t/2} - 1) = 4 - e^{-t/2}(2t + 4)\) Take the limit as \(t \rightarrow \infty\): By L'Hôpital's Rule, \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2t+4}{e^{t/2}} = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2}{\frac{1}{2}e^{t/2}} = 0\). Therefore: \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} [4 - e^{-t/2}(2t + 4)] = 4 - 0 = 4\)
questions.explanation: Express as a limit of a definite integral: \(\int_0^\infty x e^{-x/2}\,dx = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \int_0^t x e^{-x/2}\,dx\) Integrate by parts on \([0, t]\): Let \(u = x \Rightarrow du = dx\), and \(dv = e^{-x/2}dx \Rightarrow v = -2e^{-x/2}\). \(\int_0^t x e^{-x/2}\,dx = \left[ -2x e^{-x/2} \right]_0^t - \int_0^t (-2e^{-x/2})\,dx = -2t e^{-t/2} + 0 + 2 \left[ -2e^{-x/2} \right]_0^t\) \(= -2t e^{-t/2} - 4(e^{-t/2} - 1) = 4 - e^{-t/2}(2t + 4)\) Take the limit as \(t \rightarrow \infty\): By L'Hôpital's Rule, \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2t+4}{e^{t/2}} = \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{2}{\frac{1}{2}e^{t/2}} = 0\). Therefore: \(\lim_{t \rightarrow \infty} [4 - e^{-t/2}(2t + 4)] = 4 - 0 = 4\)

questions.q: Level 2 · MediumFind the minimum number of subintervals \(n\) required to guarantee that the Trapezoidal approximation of \(\int_1^3 \frac{1}{x}\,dx\) has an absolute error less than \(10^{-4}\).
questions.answer: Compute second derivative: \(f(x) = x^{-1} \Rightarrow f'(x) = -x^{-2} \Rightarrow f''(x) = 2x^{-3} = \frac{2}{x^3}\). On \([1, 3]\), \(|f''(x)| = \frac{2}{x^3}\) is decreasing, so its maximum occurs at \(x = 1\): \(K = \frac{2}{1^3} = 2\). Using the Trapezoidal error bound with \(a = 1, b = 3\): \(|E_T| \leq \frac{K(b-a)^3}{12n^2} = \frac{2(3-1)^3}{12n^2} = \frac{2(8)}{12n^2} = \frac{16}{12n^2} = \frac{4}{3n^2}.\) Require: \(\frac{4}{3n^2} \frac{4 \times 10^4}{3} = \frac{40000}{3} \approx 13333.33 \Rightarrow n > \sqrt{13333.33} \approx 115.47.\) Since \(n\) must be an integer, we require at least \(\mathbf{n = 116}\) subintervals.
questions.explanation: Compute second derivative: \(f(x) = x^{-1} \Rightarrow f'(x) = -x^{-2} \Rightarrow f''(x) = 2x^{-3} = \frac{2}{x^3}\). On \([1, 3]\), \(|f''(x)| = \frac{2}{x^3}\) is decreasing, so its maximum occurs at \(x = 1\): \(K = \frac{2}{1^3} = 2\). Using the Trapezoidal error bound with \(a = 1, b = 3\): \(|E_T| \leq \frac{K(b-a)^3}{12n^2} = \frac{2(3-1)^3}{12n^2} = \frac{2(8)}{12n^2} = \frac{16}{12n^2} = \frac{4}{3n^2}.\) Require: \(\frac{4}{3n^2} \frac{4 \times 10^4}{3} = \frac{40000}{3} \approx 13333.33 \Rightarrow n > \sqrt{13333.33} \approx 115.47.\) Since \(n\) must be an integer, we require at least \(\mathbf{n = 116}\) subintervals.

questions.q: Level 2 · Medium Evaluate the indefinite integral using partial fraction decomposition: \(\int \frac{5x - 3}{x^2 - 2x - 3}\,dx\)
questions.answer: Factor the denominator: \(x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x - 3)(x + 1)\). Set up partial fractions: \(\frac{5x - 3}{(x - 3)(x + 1)} = \frac{A}{x - 3} + \frac{B}{x + 1} \Rightarrow 5x - 3 = A(x + 1) + B(x - 3)\) Using Heaviside cover-up: Set \(x = 3\): \(5(3) - 3 = A(3 + 1) \Rightarrow 12 = 4A \Rightarrow A = 3\). Set \(x = -1\): \(5(-1) - 3 = B(-1 - 3) \Rightarrow -8 = -4B \Rightarrow B = 2\). Integrate term-by-term: \(\int \left( \frac{3}{x - 3} + \frac{2}{x + 1} \right)dx = 3\ln|x - 3| + 2\ln|x + 1| + C = \ln\left(|x - 3|^3 (x + 1)^2\right) + C\)
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x - 3)(x + 1)\). Set up partial fractions: \(\frac{5x - 3}{(x - 3)(x + 1)} = \frac{A}{x - 3} + \frac{B}{x + 1} \Rightarrow 5x - 3 = A(x + 1) + B(x - 3)\) Using Heaviside cover-up: Set \(x = 3\): \(5(3) - 3 = A(3 + 1) \Rightarrow 12 = 4A \Rightarrow A = 3\). Set \(x = -1\): \(5(-1) - 3 = B(-1 - 3) \Rightarrow -8 = -4B \Rightarrow B = 2\). Integrate term-by-term: \(\int \left( \frac{3}{x - 3} + \frac{2}{x + 1} \right)dx = 3\ln|x - 3| + 2\ln|x + 1| + C = \ln\left(|x - 3|^3 (x + 1)^2\right) + C\)

questions.q: Consider the function \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2 + 1}\). Which of the following statements describes the behavior of the function as \(x\) approaches infinity?
questions.target: Visualizing a limit numerically and graphically
questions.answer: To determine the behavior of the function \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2 + 1}\) as \(x\) approaches infinity, we consider the limit: \(\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x) = \lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{x^2 + 1}\) As \(x\) becomes very large, \(x^2\) also becomes very large. Therefore, the denominator \(x^2 + 1\) becomes very large. When the denominator of a fraction becomes infinitely large while the numerator remains constant (in this case, 1), the value of the fraction approaches 0. Thus, \(\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{x^2 + 1} = 0\). Therefore, the function approaches 0 as \(x\) approaches infinity.
questions.explanation: To determine the behavior of the function \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2 + 1}\) as \(x\) approaches infinity, we consider the limit: \(\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x) = \lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{x^2 + 1}\) As \(x\) becomes very large, \(x^2\) also becomes very large. Therefore, the denominator \(x^2 + 1\) becomes very large. When the denominator of a fraction becomes infinitely large while the numerator remains constant (in this case, 1), the value of the fraction approaches 0. questions.answer: \(abla\times\mathbf{F}=\langle0,0,1+2y\rangle\). Surface: \(z=y\) over disk \(D:x^2+y^2\leq1\). Normal upward. \(\iint_D(1+2y)dA=\pi+2\cdot0=\pi\). Wait — correct orientation gives \(\oint=3\pi/2\) after accounting for inclined surface normal. \(d\mathbf{S}=\langle0,-1,1\rangle dA\) on \(z=y\). Then \(\langle0,0,1+2y\rangle\cdot\langle0,-1,1\rangle=(1+2y)\). \(\iint_D(1+2y)dA=\pi\). Correction: \(\mathrm{curl}\mathbf{F}=\langle 0,0,1+2y\rangle\), using \(d\mathbf{S}=(-z_x,-z_y,1)dA=\langle0,-1,1\rangle dA\): integral \(=\iint(1+2y)dA=\pi(1)+0=\pi\). The answer is \(\pi\).
questions.explanation: \(abla\times\mathbf{F}=\langle0,0,1+2y\rangle\). Surface: \(z=y\) over disk \(D:x^2+y^2\leq1\). Normal upward. \(\iint_D(1+2y)dA=\pi+2\cdot0=\pi\). Wait — correct orientation gives \(\oint=3\pi/2\) after accounting for inclined surface normal. \(d\mathbf{S}=\langle0,-1,1\rangle dA\) on \(z=y\). Then \(\langle0,0,1+2y\rangle\cdot\langle0,-1,1\rangle=(1+2y)\). \(\iint_D(1+2y)dA=\pi\). questions.q: The figure shows the graph of a function \(f(x)\). What is the value of \(\lim_{x\rightarrow 2} f(x)\)?
questions.answer: The limit of a function as \(x\) approaches a certain value is the \(y\)-value that the function approaches as \(x\) gets arbitrarily close to that value. Looking at the graph, as \(x\) approaches 2 from both the left and the right, the \(y\)-value of the function approaches 2. Therefore, \(\lim_{x\rightarrow 2} f(x) = 2\).
questions.explanation: The limit of a function as \(x\) approaches a certain value is the \(y\)-value that the function approaches as \(x\) gets arbitrarily close to that value. Looking at the graph, as \(x\) approaches 2 from both the left and the right, the \(y\)-value of the function approaches 2. Therefore, \(\lim_{x\rightarrow 2} f(x) = 2\).

questions.q: Picard's theorem guarantees existence and uniqueness of IVP solution when \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial y\) are:
questions.target: Limits that fail to exist and the squeeze theorem
questions.answer: Applying Differential Equations principles, Picard-Lindelöf conditions. Therefore, the verified correct option is continuous on a neighborhood of \((x_0,y_0)\).
questions.explanation: Applying Differential Equations principles, Picard-Lindelöf conditions. Therefore, the verified correct option is continuous on a neighborhood of \((x_0,y_0)\).

questions.q: Changing the value of a Riemann-integrable \(f\) at finitely many points in \([a,b]\) leaves \(\int_a^b f\,dx\) unchanged because:
questions.target: Limits with absolute value and piecewise functions
choices: a finite set has measure zero, so it doesn't affect the integral
the antiderivative is unaffected by definition
Riemann sums always skip finite sets
questions.answer: Riemann (and Lebesgue) integration is insensitive to redefining a function on a measure-zero set — the reason FTC still applies at removable discontinuities.
questions.explanation: Riemann (and Lebesgue) integration is insensitive to redefining a function on a measure-zero set — the reason FTC still applies at removable discontinuities.

questions.q: Trig substitution \(\int\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx\) with \(x=2\sin\theta\) gives:
questions.answer: Result of trig sub for \(\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}dx=\frac{x\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}{2}+\frac{a^2}{2}\arcsin(x/a)+C\). With \(a=2\): \(\frac{x\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2}+2\arcsin(x/2)+C\).
questions.explanation: Result of trig sub for \(\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}dx=\frac{x\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}{2}+\frac{a^2}{2}\arcsin(x/a)+C\). With \(a=2\): \(\frac{x\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2}+2\arcsin(x/2)+C\).
